```{r}
library("tidyverse")
library("immunedeconv")
library("limma")
source("99_project_functions.R")

IMvigor210_plain <- readRDS("../data/IMvigor210_plain.rds")

GEP_genes <- c(
  "CD27", "CD274", "PDCD1", "CD276", "CD8A", "CMKLR1",
  "CXCL9", "CXCR6", "HLA-DQA1", "HLA-DRB1", "HLA-E",
  "IDO1", "LAG3", "NKG7", "PDCD1LG2", "PSMB10", "STAT1",
  "TIGIT"
)
```

## Data preparation

Same normalized expression as in RQ2/RQ3 (quantile normalization, then
log10(x + 1)). The GEP is the unweighted mean of the log10-transformed
GEP genes, exactly as in `GEP_score_calculation()`. It is recalculated
here from a matrix so that the unadjusted and purity-adjusted scores are
computed in exactly the same way.

```{r}
quantile_normalized <- IMvigor210_plain$counts |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  rownames_to_column("gene") |>
  quantile_normalization()

expr <- quantile_normalized |>
  column_to_rownames("gene") |>
  as.matrix()

clinical <- IMvigor210_plain$clinical
# Same patient order in expression and clinical data
clinical <- clinical[match(colnames(expr), clinical$pat_id), ]
stopifnot(identical(clinical$pat_id, colnames(expr)))

# log10(x + 1) of the quantile-normalized data (as in RQ2/RQ3)
expr_log <- log10(expr + 1)

# GEP = unweighted mean of the GEP genes (same as GEP_score_calculation)
gep_score <- function(m, genes) {
  genes <- genes[genes %in% rownames(m)]
  colMeans(m[genes, , drop = FALSE], na.rm = TRUE)
}
```

## Estimating tumor purity (ESTIMATE)

ESTIMATE is run on the TPM matrix supplied with the data, which is the
input type `immunedeconv` expects. The method is rank-based within each
sample, so it is not very sensitive to the exact scaling. The biomarkers
themselves are still calculated from the quantile-normalized data, as in
RQ2/RQ3.

```{r}
tpm <- as.matrix(IMvigor210_plain$tpm)
# Same patients, same order as the expression matrix used for the biomarkers
stopifnot(all(colnames(expr) %in% colnames(tpm)))
tpm <- tpm[, colnames(expr)]

purity_res <- deconvolute_estimate(tpm)

purity_row <- grep("purity", rownames(purity_res),
                   ignore.case = TRUE, value = TRUE)
stopifnot(length(purity_row) == 1)

tumor_purity <- as.numeric(purity_res[purity_row, ])
names(tumor_purity) <- colnames(purity_res)
tumor_purity <- tumor_purity[colnames(expr)]
stopifnot(identical(names(tumor_purity), colnames(expr)))

df <- data.frame(
  pat_id   = colnames(expr),
  TMB      = clinical$TMB,
  PD1      = expr_log["PDCD1", ],
  GEP      = gep_score(expr_log, GEP_genes),
  purity   = tumor_purity,
  Response = factor(clinical$BOR, levels = c("NR", "R"))
)
summary(df$purity)
```

## Does purity differ between response groups?

```{r}
#| fig-width: 4
#| fig-height: 4
purity_test <- wilcox.test(purity ~ Response, data = df, exact = FALSE)

df |>
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(Response)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Response, y = purity)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.12, alpha = 0.5) +
  annotate("text", x = Inf, y = Inf, hjust = 1.1, vjust = 1.5,
           label = paste0("p = ", signif(purity_test$p.value, 2))) +
  labs(x = "Response (R = complete response, NR = progressive disease)",
       y = "ESTIMATE tumor purity") +
  theme_minimal()
```

## Relationship between purity and the biomarkers

```{r}
purity_cor <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c("PD1", "GEP", "TMB"), function(v) {
  t <- cor.test(df$purity, df[[v]], method = "spearman", exact = FALSE)
  data.frame(biomarker = v, rho = unname(t$estimate), p = t$p.value,
             n = sum(complete.cases(df$purity, df[[v]])))
}))
purity_cor$p_adjusted_BH <- p.adjust(purity_cor$p, method = "BH")

purity_cor |>
  mutate(across(c(p, p_adjusted_BH), ~ format(signif(., 2)))) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2)
```

```{r}
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 3.5
biomarker_labels <- c(PD1 = "PDCD1 expression",
                      GEP = "T cell-inflamed GEP score",
                      TMB = "TMB (mut/Mb)")

df |>
  pivot_longer(c(PD1, GEP, TMB), names_to = "biomarker", values_to = "value") |>
  mutate(biomarker = factor(biomarker, levels = names(biomarker_labels))) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = purity, y = value)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~ biomarker, scales = "free_y",
             labeller = as_labeller(biomarker_labels)) +
  labs(x = "ESTIMATE tumor purity", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()
```

## Sensitivity analysis: adjusting expression for purity

As in the course exercise, the linear component of purity is removed
from the **expression matrix**, and PD-1 and the GEP are then
recalculated (the final score is not adjusted). TMB comes from DNA
sequencing and is not changed by this step.

```{r}
expr_adj <- removeBatchEffect(
  expr_log,
  covariates = matrix(df$purity, ncol = 1)
)

df_adj <- df |>
  mutate(
    PD1 = expr_adj["PDCD1", ],
    GEP = gep_score(expr_adj, GEP_genes)
  )

# Unadjusted version: same scale and same GEP definition as in RQ3
df_unadj <- df
```

```{r}
shift_table <- function(d, label) {
  do.call(rbind, lapply(c("PD1", "GEP"), function(v) {
    z <- as.numeric(scale(d[[v]]))
    is_R <- d$Response == "R"
    t <- wilcox.test(z[is_R & !is.na(is_R)], z[!is_R & !is.na(is_R)],
                     conf.int = TRUE, exact = FALSE)
    data.frame(analysis = label, biomarker = biomarker_labels[[v]],
               shift_SD = unname(t$estimate),
               CI_low = t$conf.int[1], CI_high = t$conf.int[2],
               p = t$p.value)
  }))
}

shifts <- rbind(shift_table(df_unadj, "Unadjusted"),
                shift_table(df_adj, "Purity-adjusted"))

shifts |>
  mutate(p = format(signif(p, 2))) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2)
```

```{r}
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3
ggplot(shifts, aes(x = shift_SD, y = biomarker, colour = analysis)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = CI_low, xmax = CI_high),
                  position = position_dodge(width = 0.5)) +
  labs(x = "Shift, responders vs non-responders (SD units, 95% CI)",
       y = NULL, colour = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()
```

## Does purity explain the association with response?

A logistic model asks whether the GEP still carries information about
response when purity is in the model (a regression-based alternative to
adjusting the expression matrix).

```{r}
d_mod <- df |>
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(Response)) |>
  mutate(across(c(PD1, GEP, purity), ~ as.numeric(scale(.))))

m_gep    <- glm(Response ~ GEP, data = d_mod, family = binomial)
m_gep_pu <- glm(Response ~ GEP + purity, data = d_mod, family = binomial)

or_table <- function(m, label) {
  est <- exp(cbind(coef(m), confint.default(m)))
  data.frame(model = label, term = rownames(est),
             OR = est[, 1], CI_low = est[, 2], CI_high = est[, 3],
             row.names = NULL)
}

rbind(or_table(m_gep, "GEP only"),
      or_table(m_gep_pu, "GEP + purity")) |>
  dplyr::filter(term != "(Intercept)") |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2)
```

## Interpretation

**How purity can influence PD-1 and the GEP.** In bulk RNA-seq, each gene's signal is a mixture of RNA from tumor cells and from non-tumor cells (T cells, other immune cells, fibroblasts, endothelium). PDCD1 is expressed mainly by T cells, and the GEP genes mostly reflect T cells, NK cells, antigen presentation and IFN-γ signalling. Lower-purity samples contain a larger non-tumor fraction and should therefore show higher PD-1 and GEP values even if the immune cells themselves are no more active. This is what we see: estimated purity is strongly negatively correlated with the GEP (rho = −0.73, BH-adjusted p = 3.6e-33) and with PDCD1 expression (rho = −0.63, p = 8.3e-23). The GEP is affected more than PD-1, as expected for a score that averages 18 immune genes. Because PD-1 and the GEP are strongly correlated (rho = 0.92), they are affected in nearly the same way. TMB, measured from tumor DNA, is not clearly related to purity (rho = 0.12, p = 0.15, n = 150).

**A circularity caveat.** ESTIMATE calculates purity from immune and
stromal gene sets, and some of these genes are immune genes that overlap
with, or are co-expressed with, the GEP genes. A part of the correlation
between purity and the GEP is therefore built in by construction and is
not independent evidence of a composition effect. Purity estimated from
DNA (copy-number-based methods) would avoid this, but is not available in
this dataset.

**Could purity explain the associations in RQ2 and RQ3?** Purity did not differ significantly between responders and non-responders (Wilcoxon p = 0.17), so differences in purity are unlikely to be the main explanation for the biomarker differences. After removing the linear purity component from the expression data, the responder–non-responder shift for PD-1 was unchanged (0.71 SD, 95% CI 0.36–1.05, before; 0.71 SD, 95% CI 0.31–1.13, after), and for the GEP it was slightly larger (0.84 SD, 95% CI 0.46–1.22, before; 0.97 SD, 95% CI 0.52–1.40, after). The confidence intervals overlap, so we do not interpret the small change as a real increase. The association with response therefore does not appear to be an artifact of the tumor/non-tumor ratio. Two caveats apply. First, ESTIMATE purity is itself derived from expression, so it only captures the composition variation that its gene sets can see, and some of the purity–GEP correlation is built in by construction. Second, with only 25 responders the intervals are wide.

**Would adjusting for purity necessarily improve interpretation?** No.
It depends on the question being asked.

- *Why adjustment may help:* it separates the immune signal per cell from
  the amount of immune cells in the sample, and shows whether the
  biomarker adds information beyond sample composition. It also makes
  biomarker values more comparable between samples with different tumor
  content.
- *Why adjustment may hurt:* immmune infiltration is part of the biology
  that PD-1 and the GEP are designed to capture. Removing the
  purity-associated variation removes part of the signal of interest, so
  the adjusted biomarker answers a different question ("immune signal
  beyond infiltration") than the unadjusted one. Purity may also be a
  consequence of the immune response (immune cells killing tumor cells
  and lowering purity), so adjusting for it could remove a real effect
  and does not simply correct a bias.
  
  In our data adjustment did not clearly improve anything: the PD-1 association was unchanged, with a somewhat weaker raw p-value (1.8e-4 before, 1.1e-3 after), and the GEP association was slightly stronger (0.84 to 0.97 SD), although the confidence intervals overlap. This agrees with the main point that adjusting changes the question being asked, and does not automatically give a better answer..

**Conclusion.** Tumor purity is strongly associated with the immune
biomarkers in bulk RNA-seq (rho = -0.73 for the GEP and -0.63 for PD-1),
which fits a composition effect: samples with less tumor tissue contain
more immune RNA. It does not, however, explain their association with
response. Purity did not differ significantly between responders and
non-responders (p = 0.17), and the PD-1 and GEP differences remained
after adjusting the expression data for purity and after including purity
in a logistic model, where the GEP odds ratio was, if anything, larger.
TMB, which is measured from tumor DNA, was not clearly related to
purity. Purity should therefore be reported and examined when PD-1 and
the GEP are interpreted, but it is not simply a nuisance variable to
adjust away, because immune infiltration is part of the biology these
biomarkers are meant to capture. Adjusted and unadjusted analyses are
best presented together as a sensitivity analysis. As in RQ3, these are
univariate associations in a single-arm cohort, restricted to the
extreme response groups (25 responders), and they do not show that any
biomarker predicts response in new patients.
